newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU fails to agree stance on climate change goals.
newsitem.headline: EU fails to agree stance on climate change goals.

text.p: European Union environment ministers failed late on Monday to set targets for post-2000 cuts in the bloc's emissions of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, with a deal foundering on how far and how fast to go.
"There was no deal," one EU diplomat told reporters.
"It means that tomorrow (Tuesday) we will have to tell the rest of the world that we do not have a position yet," the diplomat said.
He was referring to United Nations-backed talks in Geneva this week between more than 150 countries that were intended to seek a binding pact on cutting carbon dioxide and other gaseous emissions.
French Environment Minister Corinne Lepage said that failure while "a shame" was better than unbelievable targets.
"It was a shame but that being said, what's important in the end is that we have a realistic position which we know will be met at the EU level," Lepage told reporters.

Ministers abandoned efforts to agree a text drawn up by EU president Ireland committing the bloc's 15 countries to cuts of between five and 10 percent of greenhouse gases by the year 2005 based on 1990 levels and 10-20 percent cuts by 2010.
"We thought it was better not to push for conclusions if people weren't prepared to commit themselves to anything," a spokesman for the Irish EU presidency told reporters.

Greenhouse gases, which include methane and the chlorofluorocarbon-type substances used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants, are those gases generated in power generation, industry and transport which trap solar energy in the atmosphere in a global-warming "greenhouse effect".

One EU official said earlier that countries were divided between those wanting tougher proposals, such as Germany, Austria and Denmark, those backing the text, namely Britain, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg and Finland, and the others.
France and Sweden wanted EU offers of cuts to be based on tonnes per capita rather than on absolute figures while Spain, Portugal and Greece wanted less severe cuts.

Lepage, who said the per-capita option was also backed by Greece, Italy, Spain and Portugal, rejected suggestions that the option would pave the way for populous developing countries like China and India to avoid curbing emissions in later talks.

The EU position, once fixed, will bear on United Nations negotiators' efforts at meetings in Geneva this week and in the coming months during preparations for a binding protocol on cuts slated for agreement in 1997.
